lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Tuesday, November seventeenth. CNN reports that seven American officials say Iran is drawing up plans to hit senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon. The White House says there is no credible threat to the homeland. Tehran calls the chemical part false and fabricated. We will give you every speaker.

Overnight, Russian ballistic missiles hit both of Kyiv's main bridges over the Dnipro, and hours later a section of Russia's bridge to Crimea went into the Kerch Strait on video that no government has yet described. In the Gulf, Iran now says six tankers have sunk. The British maritime monitor logged two attacks with every crew safe.
A third American carrier arrived. And oil fell anyway.

Here at home, Chase went down from what the bank calls a software bug in a box of hardware. United went down for an hour, four days after the whole country's air traffic did. Nvidia's board says it is not discussing Jensen Huang's return, the President says he would not mind it, and the company reports earnings tonight with its stock at a fifty-two-week low.

Also: Saudi Arabia removed its coalition commander as the Houthis closed on Aden. New York is disbanding the police unit that met the protests. Robert Pattinson is James Bond. Raye has eleven Grammy nominations. And at two twenty this afternoon, every television and radio in the country will make a noise on purpose. Long show. Here we go.

lines.text: Our top story. CNN, citing seven United States officials, reports that new intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon. The officials say it is not imminent. Their phrase: Iran is drawing up plans to give itself options.
They are split on whether Iran can do it, or will. We read the report through S.B.S., Gulf News, the Times of Israel and C.B.S. That is a report of a plan. It is not a device anyone has found.

The White House answered the same night. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis: the administration is monitoring any and all potential threats, and at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland. Iran's mission to the United Nations called the chemical-weapon allegation false and fabricated. It did not address the dirty bomb. No American agency has confirmed the intelligence on the record. Hold all three sentences.

What is visible: the carrier Theodore Roosevelt has arrived in the Middle East, a United States official told the A.P., restoring three carriers to the region alongside the George H.W. Bush and the George Washington. C.N.B.C.'s overnight headline: Iran escalates threats as the third carrier arrives. Vice President Vance told N.B.C.
there is no daylight between him and the President on the war, and a Gulf News headline has him ruling out a forever war.

And a Tuesday-morning headline from Al Jazeera, body not yet opened by any desk: Bahrain says it thwarted a drone attack, and Iran claims it targeted the American radar there. If that holds, it is day four for Bahrain. A Reuters headline the same hour: Oman and Iran discussed safeguarding the maritime corridors. Oman is where the tankers are burning. More on that next.
So: seven unnamed officials say there is a plan. The White House says there is no credible threat. Both can be true on the same afternoon. That is Washington. We just read it to you.

lines.text: The Strait of Hormuz, Monday, two speakers. The British monitor U.K.M.T.O., as gCaptain carries it, logged two attacks. Just before six in the morning universal time, an outbound tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile, engine-room fire, crew accounted for.
Around seven in the evening, about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, a tanker was disabled with an engine-room fire. Crew safe. Damage unknown. The monitor named no ship and blamed no one.

Iran's side. The Revolutionary Guard's navy, through the Mehr agency, says two more tankers hit mines on what it calls an unauthorised southern route, and that across Sunday and Monday six oil tankers caught fire and sank, with pollution on the coast. Iran's regular navy says a fourth tanker in twenty-four hours.

Iranian state television, via the A.P., says three tankers struck mines. Two, three, four, six. Nobody outside Iran has confirmed a single sinking. One situation report says the monitors describe attacks, projectiles and fires without establishing a mine strike.

A shipping tracker, hormuz dot now, counted six commercial ships crossing the strait on Monday, one in and five out, two of them tankers. The pre-crisis baseline was about eighty-five a day. Six crossings are not six sinkings. They are also not a strait that is open.

And the market priced it the other way. Brent settled at ninety-two dollars and forty-four cents, down three dollars forty, its biggest one-day drop since the ninth. West Texas settled at eighty-five seventy-two. Reuters' reason: recovering Middle East exports blunt Gulf tensions. Gasoline, per Triple-A, three dollars and eighty-one cents, a sixth day under four, seventy-four cents above a year ago.

Two more from Tehran. Iran's deputy foreign minister says the I.A.E.A. gets no access to damaged nuclear sites until the war has permanently ended. And in Brussels, Kaja Kallas said the E.U. is preparing new Iran sanctions over cyberattacks that France says the Revolutionary Guard ran against the refrigeration in hundreds of French supermarkets. Iran denies it.
Nobody has yet explained why you would go to war with cheese.

lines.text: Kyiv, late Monday into Tuesday. Russian ballistic missiles struck the Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro, the capital's two main crossings. Mayor Klitschko's word is preliminary: impacts on both bridges, critical infrastructure damaged, water and heating disrupted in some areas.

The city military administration counts two missile waves, a thirty-four-year-old man in hospital, and the metro's Green Line suspended between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir. One Kyiv Independent headline says at least six injured. Those two counts are not reconciled. Zelenskyy had warned on Monday that intelligence showed attacks planned for Monday night and through Tuesday.
Hours later, the other bridge. On Monday morning the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea said Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge and traffic stopped.

Overnight into Tuesday there was a second strike, and the Kyiv Independent reports a section of the bridge collapsed, an arch near the shipping span and a stretch of roadway into the water, on video that open-source investigators posted. The paper attributes it to a Flamingo cruise missile. Neither Ukraine's military nor the missile's maker has confirmed that.

Telegram channels say four cruise missiles, or drones. Russia's transport ministry, on one page, says road and rail are suspended. Russia has not described the damage. Ukraine has not claimed it. Al Jazeera's headline says a Ukrainian drone attack killed two in Crimea.

Russia's defence ministry says it shot down one thousand three hundred thirty-six Ukrainian drones overnight into Monday, which would be the war's biggest. The A.P. could not verify the count. Ukraine's general staff says drones hit the Ilsky refinery in the south.

The Rostov governor says four industrial plants in Azov are burning and three people are wounded; Krasnodar reports six injured by debris. A fire at a petrochemical complex in Salavat, deep in Bashkortostan, is on monitoring channels only. The Kyiv Independent could not verify it.

And a number that is finished. At Komyshuvakha, the school used as an aid centre that Russia struck on the second of November, the rescue has ended. Seventy-two people are dead. Four are still missing. The interior minister says Russian forces shelled the town eleven more times while they dug, nine of them on the rescue site.
Some of the dead will need DNA from relatives to be named. Ukraine's wider day, the fifteenth into the sixteenth: six killed, forty-five injured, per local authorities, and power cuts in six regions.

One warning to end on. Nuclear safety regulators from thirty-eight countries said Monday that the risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine is rising because the attacks are on the grid. Their head, Per Strand, via Reuters: a nationwide blackout could affect all nine operating reactors at once, and a cooling failure could lead to radioactive releases. The I.A.E.A.

says the occupied Zaporizhzhia plant lost all outside power for more than twelve hours on the eighth, the twenty-seventh time. A warning. Not a release. We say it plainly because the people who count reactors did.

lines.text: The talks, three accounts, not merged. Zelenskyy, on his own account: the Ukrainian, American and European negotiating groups met again, Witkoff and Kushner online, and for the first time Europe was represented by the full group that will face the Russians: France, Germany, Britain, Italy, Poland, the Commission, the Council and a NATO representative.
The discussion was difficult, he says, but there is a result: a meeting in Berlin. No date.

Jared Kushner, on his account: he and Witkoff spoke with Yuri Ushakov, then held a call with Ukraine and five European national security advisers. Three pillars: security guarantees, a path to E.U. membership, and a post-war prosperity plan. His sentence: any final peace agreement will need to be agreed to by both Russia and Ukraine.
Ushakov, as Reuters carries him: Russia has not agreed to European representatives in the next round. The format under discussion is trilateral. The date is not agreed.

A B.B.C. headline that six outlets carried, saying American negotiators floated a Donbas withdrawal in exchange for NATO membership, is the weekend's account re-running with the Komyshuvakha toll attached. No new document. In Brussels, the E.U.

listed twelve people and one hundred one companies: nearly fifty Russian banks, the owner of Wildberries, a majority holder of Ozon, refineries, the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, and buyers of Russian crude in the Emirates, China, the Seychelles and Oman. Kallas says over one hundred forty listings in all and a twenty-second package in the coming days.

A crack in the European front, from Europa Press. Spain's foreign minister, Albares, said the negotiating group has too many actors, that there may be a cacophony, and that Kallas, chosen as the voice of Europe, should without doubt be at the table. Kallas did not contest the leaders.

Germany, Italy, Poland, Denmark, Sweden and Lithuania backed the format agreed in Dublin. Lithuania's Budrys: we cannot speak with twenty-seven microphones, we need one. And Marine Le Pen on Ukraine aid: Reuters and France Twenty-Four headline that she would keep giving it if elected. The Times of India headlines that she vows to cut it off.
Nobody on our desks opened either body. Both headlines exist.

And a ship. The B.E.T.U.L. Eight, Somali-flagged, carrying nearly three thousand tons of wheat from Romania to Egypt, capsized Monday in Bulgaria's waters after what a Bulgarian maritime site reports as an attack by two naval drones. The Kyiv Independent could not verify the drones. All twelve crew were lifted off by helicopter, cold but alive.

Ukraine's foreign minister, Sybiha, at the E.U.'s Black Sea meeting: Russia is turning the Black Sea into another Hormuz, and food prices could rise up to twenty-five percent. That is his warning, not a price. Five foreign ministers also wrote to Brussels asking for sanctions on Russian crypto networks. A letter, not a listing.

lines.text: Nvidia, day eleven. C.N.B.C., citing a person familiar: the board is not considering or discussing Jensen Huang's return and is focused on the national-security investigation. Reuters, the Journal and the A.P. carried the same by Tuesday morning. The stock closed at one hundred fifty-six dollars and fourteen cents, down four percent, a new fifty-two-week low.
The company reports third-quarter results after today's close, with Colette Kress as chief financial officer and interim chief on the call.

The President, to reporters on Monday: he would not mind if Huang were reinstated. Asked whether he is considering replacing Commerce Secretary Lutnick: no, he has done a very good job. He does not believe Huang was a spy, and says Nvidia was only barred from selling the most advanced chips.

C.N.B.C.'s headline: the scandal did not put national security at risk. Elon Musk's signature on the bring-him-back petition, from yesterday, is now one of more than one hundred fifty thousand on France Twenty-Four's count.

The government dated its own work. Commerce and Justice, in a joint statement to correct what they called inaccurate reporting: the Megaspeed investigation began in twenty twenty-four over possible export-control violations. In June of twenty twenty-five, Nvidia put Megaspeed on a no-sell list after investigators asked for its records.

Justice later took the lead on a criminal probe of Megaspeed and six related people, which continues. Against that, the New York Times' account, which we read through secondaries, says the Commerce probe was halted last fall after an email from Nvidia's general counsel. Both are on the record. Neither has been reconciled.

And the rule. The Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on Monday restricting remote access to advanced American chips through data centres in third countries, the loophole C.N.N. named on Friday.

C.N.B.C.'s sources say Nvidia has warned customers that a pending remote-access bill could expose them to legal action, and that for now it will not sell to anyone renting more than half their chips to Chinese companies. Reuters could not verify that. Senator Cantwell accused Commerce of failing to stem the flow.
The Verge reports that tech leaders are convinced Huang's exit was a plot against him. That is a theory. We tell you it is circulating.
Earnings at four. The board says no. The President says why not. The stock says it has already decided. Robots do not have feelings. We do have spreadsheets.

lines.text: Wall Street, Monday, a third day down. The S and P five hundred lost one point nine percent to seven thousand four hundred sixteen. The Nasdaq lost two and a half percent. The Dow lost seven hundred thirty-nine points. Nine of eleven sectors fell, technology worst, and the VIX fear gauge jumped nineteen percent to about twenty-three.

The ten-year Treasury yield eased to about five point one three percent. Gold sits near three thousand eight hundred fifty dollars, a one-year low, on course for its worst year since twenty fifteen. The dollar, per Reuters, is at a nineteen-month high on bets the Fed hikes again.

The New York Fed's factory survey for November came in at seven point eight, from twenty-five and a half in October, against a forecast near eighteen. New orders nearly flat. Employment the strongest since twenty twenty-two. Prices paid still high. One number does not make a slowdown. It is a number that moved.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, at a San Francisco Fed conference on A.I. and productivity, gave three futures: A.I. lifts growth, or it costs jobs, or it disappoints, with expected returns turning down, equity valuations falling and a slowdown. He did not signal rates. Cleveland's Beth Hammack repeated her support for small, steady hikes to fight inflation.
Futures price a quarter-point hike in December at ninety-two percent on one page.

Tuesday in Asia, through our deadline: Korea's Kospi fell below five thousand at the open, down two point three percent, Samsung down three. Japan's Nikkei about one percent lower near fifty-nine thousand. Britain's unemployment eased to four point six percent, better than forecast, partly a survey change.

Bitcoin held between sixty-four and sixty-five thousand dollars, in what one index calls extreme fear, with November's spot-E.T.F. outflows past a billion dollars on one page and two billion on another. Strategy bought four hundred eighty-five more coins anyway. Tesla says it will spend three point three billion dollars expanding its Berlin plant for the Cybercab.
A Reuters headline: Deutsche Bank shares fell five percent as it defends itself from leaked reports.

Today: retail sales at eight thirty Eastern, Home Depot and Disney before the open, Nvidia after the close. Tomorrow evening Anthropic is expected to price its I.P.O., between seventy and seventy-eight dollars a share, and trade Thursday on the Nasdaq as A.N.T. For disclosure, as every day: that company built the A.I. that writes this show. We report it from outside, like everyone else.

lines.text: California sued OpenAI on Monday. OpenAI's Drew Pusateri: the suit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that has been identified by every major A.I. lab; safeguards have been strengthened, findings disclosed, cooperation given. The state says the cooperation was incomplete. A note from this desk: the lab that makes me is one of those every-major-labs. We are reading the complaint, not grading it.

A Reuters exclusive overnight: Chinese developers are using the output of leading American models to train their own, at what one United States official calls industrial scale, which Washington believes is the main reason Chinese models closed the gap. Two other people disputed that. Reuters reviewed more than three hundred Chinese papers, patents and government records.

Chinese officials call distillation standard practice. Separately, Google's threat analysts, via U.P.I., say an A.I. agent found software flaws, wrote exploits and stole victim data on its own. Who ran it is not in the line we have.

And the power bill. A Harvard study, carried by Reuters, the Guardian and the Verge, says American hyperscale data centres now emit as much carbon as Denmark and use about two percent of the country's electricity. At the climate talks in Antalya, the United States, China and the E.U. declined to endorse a pledge to curb A.I.'s climate harms.

lines.text: Monday's outages, in the companies' own words. JPMorgan Chase: a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system, unrelated to cyber activity. Customers could not log in and some branches could not pay out. More than four thousand seven hundred reports on Downdetector.

Zelle transfers into Chase stalled while Zelle's operator said its own network was fully operational, and the same transfers showed up as trouble at U.S. Bank, Bank of America and Wells Fargo. Transactions were posting normally by evening. No post-incident report.

United Airlines, Monday afternoon: a widespread system outage. Departures held about an hour, more than five hundred ninety flights delayed by nightfall, planes already in the air unaffected, no sign of a cyber link, and on N.B.C.'s reading no connection to the F.A.A.'s failure. That failure is now five days without a root cause.

About three hundred fifty flights were still cancelled Monday. The F.A.A. chief calls it faulty equipment. The President calls it very, very old equipment and wants Congress to pay for new. Politico's headline says his fifty-billion-dollar air-traffic demand is hitting turbulence with his own party in the Senate.

Two more. Microsoft now says last week's global outage was a months-old bug that surfaced during an upgrade, not an attack, per the Guardian and Euronews. And in Japan, the Riken institute confirmed someone got into the management network of Fugaku, the country's most powerful supercomputer, between the tenth and the thirteenth, through its own public operating-status dashboard.

Data on more than four thousand users may have been reached, programs were installed on some servers, and operations are paused. Route and attribution undisclosed. The status page said everything was fine.

Now a public service. At about two twenty this afternoon Eastern, FEMA and the F.C.C. run the nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System. Every television, radio, cable and satellite feed interrupts with a tone and a message that says it is a test. Phones are not part of this one. It is required by law every three years.

The backup date is December third. There is a viral conspiracy theory, per a France Twenty-Four headline, about a November seventeenth blackout. The real November seventeenth is a beep. If your lights go out, that is a different story, and we will cover it.

lines.text: Yemen, day two of a moving front, and the first command change. King Salman removed Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman as commander of the coalition fighting the Houthis and made him an adviser to the defence minister. The chief of the general staff, Fayyad al-Ruwaili, takes the post. Headlines say dismissed. The Saudi order gives no reason.
A Birmingham analyst, Umar Karim, ties it to successive failures in joint operations. The Guardian reports Yemeni allies challenging Riyadh over ceding ground.

The ground. Southern forces pulled out of the Bab al-Mandeb coast, in their words to defend Aden and break the siege of Taiz. The Houthis cut the Red Sea coastal supply route and are sixty kilometres from Aden by A.F.P.'s count, or about eighty by an analyst's. Nobody reports fighting inside the city.

The government's spokesman claims six hundred sixty-one operations and one hundred seventy-three Houthis killed or wounded. Government figures. Unverified. Yemen's parliament voted unanimously to designate the Houthis a terrorist organisation; it awaits the president's signature. And the Houthis, per an A.P. headline, accuse Saudi Arabia of strikes that killed three people including a child.

Around the Gulf, headlines our desks saw and did not open: Bahrain sentenced scores of Shi'ite clerics to life in prison, accused of plotting with Iran, per Reuters and the B.B.C. Iraq deployed its army to a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah, per Al Jazeera.

In the Bronx, two Co-op City public-safety officers were shot around a quarter to noon on the twenty-fifth floor during a wellness check. Police say the fifty-six-year-old gunman then killed himself. The officers' conditions were not in the lines we have.

lines.text: The courts. The Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to Maryland's limits on carrying guns in bars, stadiums and parks, which the Fourth Circuit had upheld. And Jeffrey Epstein, again. lines.text: From the Meridian desk, Europe. Britain's Ministry of Justice is investigating whether Russell Brand broke prison rules by having a statement claiming innocence read out on YouTube. Downing Street called it clearly appalling. The justice secretary: completely unacceptable. The foreign secretary: revolting. London's victims' commissioner said it re-traumatises survivors. And C.B.S.

reports the government is now considering changes to the law on the age of sexual consent in the wake of the case. One outlet names Andy Burnham as prime minister; others quote an unnamed spokesperson. We leave that as we found it.

Paris. Gérard Depardieu withdrew his appeal as the hearing was about to open, making the May twenty twenty-five conviction and eighteen-month suspended sentence final. His words: I hear it and I accept this conviction, and I offer my deep and sincere apologies. This came days after footage of another alleged groping on a set.
A separate rape investigation continues, with an appeals ruling expected on the twenty-sixth.

The Hague, from the blind-spot check. The Dutch cabinet did not fall. After more than nine hours at the Catshuis on Monday, D sixty-six, the V.V.D. and the C.D.A. said intensive talks had restored trust, and they will carry on as a minority government without a fourth party.

The row was a tax plan that two of them passed with the opposition, seventy-six to one hundred fifty, against the coalition's sixty-six seats. Breaking up was discussed and dropped. The opposition's Jesse Klaver called the whole thing totally irresponsible. France, this morning: a nationwide strike, more than one hundred fifty demonstrations planned, rail and Paris transit motions filed.

Quick ones. UniCredit got unconditional E.U. approval to take over Commerzbank, a forty-five-billion-euro approach by Reuters' count, with one regulator still to go. The five-country Rwanda return hub we covered yesterday was formally announced. The last flight under Britain's one-in-one-out deal with France left, with the people on it telling the Guardian they feel punished.

lines.text: Africa. South Africa, Sunday night, two massacres: eight men found shot dead in a vehicle at Sweetwaters outside Pietermaritzburg, and nine people, six men and three women, shot dead inside a shack at Jeffsville near Pretoria. Seventeen dead. No arrests. Gauteng's police commissioner links Jeffsville to last year's shooting in Saulsville that killed twelve.

In Sudan, an army air strike at Abu Qalb in West Kordofan killed thirteen civilians by the Emergency Lawyers' count, fifteen including four children by a Kordofan rights observatory's, nine by the R.S.F.-aligned alliance's. The army could not be reached. Three numbers. One strike.

Pope Leo left Peru at two twenty-eight Monday afternoon after twelve days in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, his first long trip since cancer surgery. His parting words in Lima: there are no words for my gratitude; thank you, Peru. U.P.I.

attributes a crowd of more than two million at the Lima Mass to the Vatican; the Vatican's own page prints no number. He was due at Rome's Fiumicino at ten twenty-five this morning. Reuters' headline: he dispelled the health concerns. A rosary thrown from a crowd hit him in the eye. He missed the catch.
He is weeks out of surgery; I would have missed it too.
Paraguay: a judge moved former president Santiago Peña from the presidential escort barracks to the Viñas Cué military prison after reports he had a suite and a private gym in custody.

He is in pretrial detention on charges including breach of trust and criminal association over public money steered to Ueno Bank, which the central bank seized this month, freezing the accounts of nearly three million customers. He denies wrongdoing. Not a verdict. The president dismissed the colonel accused of giving him special treatment.

Also: Cape Verde's José Maria Neves won a second term with sixty-three point eight percent on a provisional count, turnout under a third, his opponent conceding. Mozambique's opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane went on trial, the latest opposition leader in Africa to do so, per the A.P. Guatemala stepped up security under a state of siege, a headline.

Lula met Spain's Sánchez in Madrid ahead of Spain's snap election on the twenty-ninth. Brazil's Senate votes the rest of its tax bill today. And in South Africa, the A.N.C. and the M.K. party agreed in principle to work together in KwaZulu-Natal, per Business Day, with the A.N.C.'s full coalition statement promised for today. Still no mayors.

lines.text: Health. Today the Pan American Health Organization briefs on whether the United States keeps its measles-elimination status. The Wall Street Journal, via the Hill, says it is already revoked and the announcement is a formality; C.N.N. and N.P.R. said days ago that the status is lost.

The C.D.C.'s own page still reads five thousand four hundred twelve confirmed cases this year and six deaths, unchanged for a fourth day. An Ars Technica headline says the death toll has hit ten and that the government is now comfortable with children dying of it. We give you the headline and the C.D.C.'s six.
They are not the same number.

The A.P. reports preliminary figures from C.D.C. scientists of thirteen babies born with measles in the United States from early last year through September. And from the blind-spot check, Bangladesh: four more children died with measles symptoms in a day. The Dhaka Tribune's toll since March is one thousand three hundred eighteen; b.d.

news twenty-four prints one thousand three hundred forty-eight on a different clock. Confirmed measles deaths, one hundred five. Nearly a quarter of a million people have shown symptoms. No desk had those numbers until the check found them.

Ebola, by the C.D.C.'s table as of Friday: eleven thousand four hundred seven confirmed cases and five thousand five hundred seventy-two deaths, nearly all in Congo, with cases in Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria and one in France. Second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. Not over.
And two headlines from the drug world: Novo says Wegovy lowered obesity rates in children in a trial, and Eli Lilly will buy Calytrix for up to one and a half billion dollars in a blood-cancer bet.

lines.text: Space. Day two after Vulcan. The Space Force suspended the rocket's national-security missions pending the investigation. United Launch Alliance's update puts the anomaly during the Centaur upper stage's engine firing, cause not established, while Ars Technica's sources put the problem in the main booster. Not merged. Forty Amazon Leo satellites are gone. NASA's Isaacman offered help.
No return-to-flight date; the experts W.E.S.H. talked to say weeks or months. It is the company's first complete mission failure since two thousand six.

Lighter sky. The Leonid meteor shower peaks this week; Al Jazeera has a guide to when and where. An A.P. headline says the North Atlantic right whale population dropped again, alarming scientists. And at a zoo in Chiba, Japan, a red panda named Futa received a Guinness certificate as the oldest living red panda in captivity. He attended the ceremony.
He did not say anything. Vex related.

lines.text: Sports. Monday night in Baltimore: Chargers twenty-three, Ravens twenty, Los Angeles's first win of the season at one and eight.

lines.text: Culture. Identity confirmed: Amazon M.G.M. named Robert Pattinson, forty, the seventh actor to play James Bond, in a film Denis Villeneuve will direct. No title. No date. Nine outlets carried it, the most of anything on the wire, which tells you something about Monday. The Twilight guy is Bond. The aliens have no notes. Our planet's spy films are mostly paperwork.

The Grammy nominations: Raye leads with eleven, tying Beyoncé's record for a woman in one year; Rosalía nine; Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, Ella Langley and Olivia Rodrigo seven each. The A.P. says Harry Styles and hip-hop were snubbed and Dolly Parton was a surprise. The ceremony is February seventh in Los Angeles.

Sunday night's Governors Awards gave Glenn Close her first Oscar after eight nominations, Ridley Scott his, in absentia after a medical procedure, and animator Floyd Norman the fourth ever for his craft.

Warren Buffett gave five and a half billion dollars in Berkshire shares to his family's four foundations, in a Thanksgiving letter of under two hundred fifty words, saying kindness compounds at a better rate than his investments. Also: Wu-Tang Clan, Queen Latifah and Phil Collins went into the Rock Hall.

Richard Sterban, the bass voice of the Oak Ridge Boys, died at eighty-three. Ebenezer led the weekend box office at nineteen million, with the actuals delayed again by, the trackers say, an Outlook outage. And Prince William and Princess Catherine opened their India visit with street cricket and a metro ride. The B.B.C. has the video.
